name: The Varsity Beast

inspiration.oldScript: The beast within as manhood's dark side, celebrated when he wins the game.
inspiration.newLens: The 'be a man' pressure itself, passed down three generations. The Best ending lets him be soft, and he tap-dances in the revue.

logline: Glimmer Falls High's star quarterback has one week to become a man before the Halloween Monster Bowl. Something inside him has decided to become a wolf instead.
backstory: Brick Delaney is seventeen, six foot three, and the best quarterback Glimmer Falls High has had since his father, Duke Delaney, won state in 1966 and then sold cars on the strength of it for twenty years. Duke wakes Brick at five every morning for the Delaney Man Plan: drills, raw eggs, and three rules taped to the fridge. Delaneys don't cry. Delaneys don't quit. Delaneys don't dance. The last rule is personal. Duke's own father, Augie "Featherfoot" Delaney, was a tap dancer who headlined the old Rialto, the theatre that became the Glitter Box, and Duke spent his whole childhood being mocked for it until he swore his son would never be soft. Brick has been holding himself together like a clenched fist for years. This Halloween week, with the Heartstone amplifying every feeling on Crystal Street, everything Brick is not allowed to feel has turned into fur and teeth. When the pressure peaks (a coach screaming, a crowd chanting, his father going silent), Brick becomes the Varsity Beast: a seven-foot wolf in a shredded letterman jacket, his helmet cracked over its ears, hunting anyone who looks soft. The Monster Bowl against Pine Ridge is Friday night, Halloween, and the whole town will be watching.

centralIssue.title: The pressure to be a man
centralIssue.summary: Brick is not a monster. He is a gentle kid crushed by three generations of "be a man," and the Beast is everything he has been forced to swallow. Beating him only proves his father's rules right. He needs permission, from his family and his town, to be soft.

poster: A towering wolf in a shredded maroon and gold letterman jacket and a cracked football helmet with ears bursting through, howling under stadium floodlights and a full moon over a small-town football field, a bonfire and packed bleachers behind, a teenage crew in Halloween costumes in the end zone
portrait: Close portrait of a huge gray-furred wolf wearing a cracked maroon football helmet, number 33 on a torn jersey, eyes glowing like stadium floodlights, a single tear tracking through the fur of a young, frightened face
endingPhoto: A towering wolf in a shredded maroon and gold letterman jacket and a cracked football helmet howling at midfield under stadium floodlights and a full moon, the scoreboard reading home 13, a bonfire behind the bleachers, cheerleaders and teens scattering from the end zone with pom-poms and a megaphone
taunts: Big boys don't cry. Big boys don't do anything.
You look soft. I can smell soft.
MAN UP. MAN UP. MAN UP.

clues.title: The secret playbook
clues.hint: Brick Delaney trains at Pump Iron Gym every morning at five, and he never leaves without the same spiral notebook.

encounter.title: Locker 33
encounter.place: Locker room, Pump Iron Gym and Aerobics
encounter.text: Locker 33 at Pump Iron is held shut with athletic tape and hope. Inside, under a protein shaker and a letterman jacket that smells like menthol rub, is a spiral notebook labeled PLAYS, PRIVATE. Down the hall the aerobics class is doing grapevines to a synth beat, and a radio is counting down to the Monster Bowl. Brick will be back from the showers in five minutes.
encounter.art: A steamy gym locker room, a dented gray locker held shut with strips of white athletic tape, its door cracked open on a protein shaker, a maroon and gold letterman jacket and a spiral notebook peeking out underneath, a teenager reaching for the notebook and glancing over their shoulder, steam drifting from the shower doorway, flat fluorescent light, medium shot

choices.label: Ask Moose what Brick keeps in that notebook

success.text: Moose looks at his knitting for a long time. "Those aren't plays," he says. "I mean, they look like plays. X's and O's. But the X's are feet. Shuffle, ball-change, flap. He's been writing tap routines since we were twelve." He hands you one torn-out page: a perfect time step, drawn like a quarterback sneak.
success.alone: You flip the notebook open and look at it for a long time. Those aren't plays. They look like plays, X's and O's, but the X's are feet. Shuffle, ball-change, flap. Somebody has been writing tap routines in here for years. One torn-out page slips loose into your hand: a perfect time step, drawn like a quarterback sneak.
success.art: A huge gentle lineman sitting on a locker room bench with half-knitted maroon yarn in his lap, handing over a notebook page of football diagrams labeled with dance steps

failure.text: Moose shakes his head. "Not mine to tell." Then Brick comes around the corner, towel around his neck, sees you by his locker, and goes so still and so quiet that the fluorescent tube above him pops. For a second, his shadow on the tile has ears.
failure.alone: You hesitate with your hand on the tape. Then Brick comes around the corner, towel around his neck, sees you by his locker, and goes so still and so quiet that the fluorescent tube above him pops. For a second, his shadow on the tile has ears.
failure.art: A tall teenage quarterback with a towel around his neck frozen in a locker room doorway, a fluorescent light bursting overhead, his shadow on the tiles showing wolf ears

choices.label: Open the notebook and read fast before he's back

success.text: X's and O's, arrows and loops, and in the margins in tiny careful letters: shuffle, ball-change, flap, wings. Every play is a tap routine. On the last page, pressed so hard the pen tore through: I'M SO TIRED OF BEING SCARY. You snap an instant photo and slide the notebook back with ten seconds to spare.
success.art: A notebook page covered in football X's and O's with tiny dance step notes in the margins, the words so tired of being scary pressed through the paper, a fresh instant photo developing beside it

failure.text: The notebook falls open to a page of claw marks, five deep grooves torn through the paper. A low growl comes from the showers, and then the sound of a big teenager crying very quietly so that nobody will hear. You put the notebook back and leave before either of you has to be embarrassed.
failure.art: A notebook page slashed by five deep claw marks lying on a locker room bench, steam and a hunched shadow visible through the shower doorway

choices.label: Offer to spot Brick on the bench press and just talk

success.text: You spot him and say nothing clever. Somewhere around rep twelve he says, "Do you ever just want to stop being the thing everybody needs?" Then he shows you the notebook himself: tap routines drawn like football plays, years of them. "Don't tell my dad," he says, and almost smiles.
success.art: A teenager spotting a big quarterback on a bench press in a dawn-lit gym, the quarterback sitting up afterward and shyly showing an open notebook

failure.text: The bar is heavier than you are. Brick catches it one-handed before it pins you, and for a moment his knuckles are furred and his nails are long and black. He slams the bar onto the rack and walks out without a word.
failure.art: A furred hand with long black nails gripping a loaded barbell above a startled teenager on a weight bench, gym mirrors reflecting a hulking shadow

clues.title: Duke's yearbook
clues.hint: The trophy case at Glimmer Falls High is a shrine to the 1966 state champions, and the yearbook office keeps every copy since 1959.

encounter.title: The Shrine
encounter.place: Trophy case and yearbook office, Glimmer Falls High
encounter.text: The trophy case outside the gym glows like a chapel: the 1966 state trophy, a game ball signed DUKE, and the banner the boosters hang every October, MAN UP, PROSPECTORS. Next door the yearbook office is unlocked and smells of rubber cement. The 1966 Glimmer Light sits on a shelf with its spine cracked open at a single page.
encounter.art: A high school hallway at dusk, a glass trophy case glowing warm gold with a 1966 state trophy and a signed leather football under a maroon cloth pennant, beside it the open door of a cluttered yearbook office with an old school annual lying open on a shelf, a teenager standing between them, warm case light and dim hallway, medium wide shot

choices.label: Open the yearbook to the cracked-spine page

success.text: Senior portrait: Duke Delaney, crew cut, hard eyes. Under it, his chosen quote: "My father dances. I win." Someone has doodled a tiny pair of tap shoes in the margin, and someone else has scratched them out so hard the paper tore. Three generations of hurt in one square inch.
success.art: A 1966 yearbook page with a crew-cut senior portrait and a printed quote, a tiny doodle of tap shoes in the margin violently scratched out

failure.text: The yearbook flops open to the team photo, and every 1966 Prospector in it has turned his head toward you. In the back row, young Duke is not smiling, and his eyes are wet. The book slams itself shut, and the office suddenly smells like wet dog.
failure.art: A black and white 1966 football team photo where every player has turned to stare out of the page, one young player in the back row with wet eyes

choices.label: Ask Coach Pruitt what the football staff says about Brick

success.text: Coach Pruitt marches you into the field house and points at Coach Hollings's whiteboard: BRICK. NO CRYING. NO QUITTING. NO SOFTNESS. Below it, in a different hand: HE HAS TO BE A MAN BY FRIDAY. D.D. Pruitt photographs it. "I have been yelling at that man about this for years," she says. "Let's yell louder." On the way out, she pulls Duke's 1966 yearbook off the office shelf and tucks it under your arm.
success.art: A big fierce softball coach pointing at a field house whiteboard covered in harsh rules in marker, a teenager beside her holding a camera

failure.text: Coach Hollings catches you instead. He blows his whistle in your face, calls you "sweetheart" like it's an insult, and writes you up for loitering. From the locker room, over the slam of the door, something howls right along with his whistle.
failure.art: A red-faced football coach in a maroon windbreaker blowing a whistle at a teenager in a school hallway, a locker room door shaking behind him

clues.title: Featherfoot's tap shoes
clues.hint: The Glitter Box used to be the old Rialto, and its lobby still remembers who headlined.

encounter.title: Featherfoot
encounter.place: The lobby, The Glitter Box Playhouse
encounter.text: The Glitter Box lobby is a hall of fame in sequins and dust. Between a poster for the 1977 Miss Glitter Pageant and a signed photo of a 1950s torch singer hangs an old black-and-white of a skinny young man mid-leap, tails flying: AUGIE "FEATHERFOOT" DELANEY, THE RIALTO, 1946. Below it, in a glass box, sits a pair of tap shoes so big they look like they belong to a boy who never stopped growing.
encounter.art: A sparkly small theater lobby wall crowded with old framed show photographs, a black-and-white photo of a skinny young tap dancer mid-leap in tails, a glass box below it holding a pair of huge worn black tap shoes, a tall drag queen with a platinum bouffant wig and pins in her mouth beside a teenager looking at the shoes, warm gold lobby light, medium shot

choices.label: Ask Glory about the dancer in the photo

success.text: "Featherfoot? He taught me my first time step in 1953, when I was eleven and nobody else would." Glory unlocks the case. "His son Duke left these at the stage door in 1966. Said his old man had embarrassed him enough. Augie cried for a week. Gentlest man I ever knew, and the strongest."
success.alone: The old ticket-taker shuffles over with her keys. "Featherfoot? He taught half the kids in this town their first time step, back when nobody else would." She unlocks the case. "His son Duke left these at the stage door in 1966. Said his old man had embarrassed him enough. Augie cried for a week. Gentlest man I ever knew, and the strongest."
success.art: A drag queen in a sequined robe unlocking a glass case in a theatre lobby and lifting out a pair of old tap shoes, a misty smile on her face

failure.text: Glory is mid-fitting with six pins in her mouth and waves you off. When you lean close to the glass, the tap shoes begin to tap all on their own: a soft, sad shuffle. A dancer's shadow crosses the old photo and is gone. You decide to come back when someone else is around.
failure.alone: Everyone who works here is backstage at a fitting, and nobody answers when you call. When you lean close to the glass, the tap shoes begin to tap all on their own: a soft, sad shuffle. A dancer's shadow crosses the old photo and is gone. You decide to come back when someone else is around.
failure.art: A pair of empty tap shoes tapping by themselves inside a glass case, a faint dancer's shadow sliding across an old photograph above

choices.label: Borrow the shoes and try a step on the empty stage

success.text: The shoes flop on you like clown shoes, but the stage loves them. Your clumsy shuffle comes back off the walls as a crisp, joyful rhythm, as if someone is dancing right beside you. Tucked inside the left toe is a folded note in shaky pencil: For my grandson, whoever he turns out to be. Love, Pop.
success.art: A teenager in leg warmers and oversized tap shoes on an empty glittery stage under one work light, a faint ghostly dancer in tails tapping beside them

failure.text: You trip on the very first step and slide across the stage on your back. Frankie leans out of the lighting booth, says "Ten out of ten, no notes," and makes you put the shoes back in the case. You never got to look inside them.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled on their back on a glittery stage in giant tap shoes, a stage manager in a headset leaning out of a lighting booth applauding

signature.title: Two-a-Days
signature.place: The practice field, Glimmer Falls High, midnight
signature.text: You cut across the practice field at midnight and the stadium lights slam on, every bank at once. A whistle shrieks. Something huge is running suicides on the forty-yard line, goal line and back, goal line and back, its letterman jacket shredded across its shoulders. It stops. It sniffs the air. Over the PA, a man's recorded voice says, "Walk it off, son. Walk it off."
signature.art: A high school practice field at midnight under blazing floodlights, a hulking seven-foot gray wolf in a shredded maroon and gold letterman jacket and a cracked maroon football helmet sprinting along the white yard lines, a whistle on a lanyard lying on the grass, a small teenager frozen at the chain-link fence, hard white light and black sky, wide shot

choices.label: Sprint for the bleachers and climb

success.text: You hit the bleachers and climb three rows at a time while the Beast's claws gouge the aluminum behind you. At the top row it stops, panting, ears flat, and looks up at you with something that is almost embarrassment. Then it lopes off into the dark, still running drills.
success.art: A teenager at the top of aluminum bleachers at night, a huge wolf in a letterman jacket stopped a few rows below with its ears flat, claw scratches down the seats

failure.text: You slip on the dew-wet grass and the Beast is over you, breath like hot sports drink and fear. It doesn't bite. It shoves you, hard, the way linemen shove, and roars "GET UP" in a voice that is almost Brick's. You limp home shaped like one big bruise.
failure.art: A huge wolf in a shredded jersey standing over a teenager sprawled on wet turf under floodlights, roaring down at them

choices.label: Grab the dropped whistle and call a time-out

success.text: You blow the whistle and make a T with your hands. The Beast freezes mid-stride, trained to the bone. It stands there, chest heaving, waiting to be told what to do. "Water break," you say. It sits down on the bench, very carefully, and you swear it sighs.
success.art: A teenager making a time-out T with their hands, a whistle in their mouth, a giant wolf in a letterman jacket sitting obediently on a team bench under floodlights

failure.text: The whistle is slick with dew and your blast comes out a squeak. The Beast hears weakness in it, and weakness is the one thing it was built to hunt. It chases you off the field and through two backyards, howling, and you hide in a doghouse until the lights click off.
failure.art: A teenager crammed inside a backyard doghouse at night, a wolf's huge shadow passing over the fence, stadium lights glowing in the distance

signature.title: The Bonfire Rally
signature.place: The pep rally bonfire, behind Prospector Stadium
signature.text: The Monster Bowl pep rally bonfire is three stories tall and burning a Pine Ridge dummy in effigy. The boosters have the crowd chanting BE A MAN, BE A MAN, BE A MAN, and with every chant the shape at the edge of the firelight gets bigger: shoulders, claws, a cracked helmet with ears forcing through. Duke Delaney stands on a flatbed with a bullhorn, leading the chant, not looking at it.
signature.art: A towering high school pep rally bonfire at night behind a stadium, a chanting crowd in maroon and gold sweatshirts with fists in the air, a broad middle-aged man with a crew cut on a flatbed truck shouting into a bullhorn, a teenager holding a cheer megaphone, and at the edge of the firelight a huge shape growing broad shoulders, claws and a cracked football helmet with wolf ears forcing through, orange firelight, wide shot

choices.label: Grab the cheer squad's megaphone and change the chant

success.text: "BE YOURSELF!" you scream. It sounds dumb. Then Chip, class president, grabs the other megaphone and yells it too, and the cheer squad picks it up because it's fun to shout and has a better rhythm anyway. In the dark, the shape shrinks, ears folding. Duke lowers the bullhorn, confused.
success.alone: "BE YOURSELF!" you scream. It sounds dumb. Then a kid in a class-council sweater grabs the other megaphone and yells it too, and the cheer squad picks it up because it's fun to shout and has a better rhythm anyway. In the dark, the shape shrinks, ears folding. Duke lowers the bullhorn, confused.
success.art: A teenager and a preppy class president shouting into megaphones in front of a bonfire, cheerleaders joining in, a wolf silhouette at the edge of the light shrinking

failure.text: Your megaphone squeals feedback and the crowd boos you, laughing, and the laughter feeds the Beast like gasoline. It rises out of the dark ten feet tall and roars, and the bonfire leans away from it. Everyone screams, then cheers, because they think it's the mascot.
failure.art: A ten-foot wolf in a cracked football helmet rising behind a bonfire roaring, a crowd cheering wildly as if it were a mascot, a teenager with a squealing megaphone

choices.label: Slip out of the firelight and find Brick before the Beast does

success.text: Behind the bleachers, Brick is on his knees, half changed, fur coming and going like TV static. "Make them stop," he whispers. You sit with him in the dirt. You don't tell him to man up. The chanting goes on, but here, just for a minute, his hands are only hands.
success.art: A teenager sitting beside a kneeling quarterback under dark bleachers, his arms flickering between fur and skin, bonfire light leaking through the slats

failure.text: You find the Beast instead. It pins you to the bleacher struts with one huge paw, nose to nose, and growls "Don't look at me" in a voice that cracks in the middle. Then it's gone, and your jacket hangs off you in four long stripes.
failure.art: A wolf in a cracked helmet pinning a teenager against steel bleacher struts nose to nose in the dark, firelight through the gaps

signature.title: Surfin' Route 49
signature.place: Route 49 in Lyle's Pizza delivery van, after midnight
signature.text: You catch a ride home from the late session at Pump Iron in Lyle's Pizza delivery van, sitting on a stack of flat boxes, when something lands on the roof hard enough to dent it. In the side mirror a huge furry shape is crouched on top of the giant fiberglass pizza, letterman jacket flapping, arms out like a surfer, howling at the moon. Behind you a muscle car full of linebackers is honking and chanting, "WOLF! WOLF! WOLF!" Lyle grips the wheel. "Kid," he says carefully, "there's a werewolf on my pizza."
signature.art: A pizza delivery van speeding down a moonlit country highway after midnight with a giant fiberglass pizza on its roof, a huge gray wolf in a flapping maroon letterman jacket crouched on top of the pizza with arms spread wide howling at the moon, a teenager leaning out the side window, a muscle car full of shouting football players chasing behind with headlights blazing, full moon, wide shot

choices.label: Climb out the window and surf the pizza with him

success.text: You haul yourself up and get your feet under you on the fiberglass pepperoni. The Beast looks at you, startled, then grins with way too many teeth. You surf Route 49 side by side, arms out, wind roaring, and for one stupid, glorious mile he is laughing, a real teenage laugh, with nobody keeping score. At the Glimmer Falls exit he leaps off into the orchards, still laughing.
success.art: A teenager and a huge laughing wolf in a letterman jacket surfing side by side on a giant fiberglass pizza atop a speeding van, arms out, a full moon and orchards rushing past

failure.text: You get one knee on the roof and the van hits a pothole. You spend the next mile hugging the giant fiberglass pizza like a koala while the Beast howls in your ear and the linebackers behind you take bets. Lyle drops you at home windblown and green, with pizza sauce somehow in your hair.
failure.art: A windblown teenager clinging to a giant fiberglass pizza on a speeding van roof like a koala, a howling wolf in a letterman jacket crouched beside them, football players cheering from a muscle car behind

choices.label: Talk Lyle into easing onto the shoulder, slow and steady

success.text: "Signal, brake gently, easy does it," you coach, and Lyle rolls onto the gravel shoulder like he's delivering a wedding cake. The muscle car roars past, booing. With the chanting gone, the shape on the roof goes quiet. You hear a soft thump, claws on gravel, and then a voice that is almost Brick's says, "Thanks for the ride," from the dark of the orchard.
success.art: A pizza delivery van parked on a gravel road shoulder at night, a muscle car's taillights disappearing ahead, a large wolf shape loping quietly into a moonlit orchard, a teenager leaning out the passenger window

failure.text: Lyle panics and stomps the brakes. The Beast sails off the roof, lands on all fours in the headlights and turns, eyes stadium white. The linebackers pile out of the muscle car cheering, the Beast charges the noise, and everyone scatters into a pumpkin patch, you included.
failure.art: A huge wolf in a torn letterman jacket landing on all fours in the glare of van headlights, glowing white eyes, teenagers and football players scattering into a moonlit pumpkin patch

choices.label: Lean out the window and yell that he doesn't have to win this one

success.text: "Hey! You don't have to show them anything!" you yell over the wind. "It's just a ride!" The howling stops. The Beast hunkers down on the pizza, and you swear its ears go soft. When the muscle car swerves past chanting, it doesn't even turn its head. At a red light it slides down the windshield, gives Lyle a sheepish little wave and lopes off.
success.art: A wolf in a letterman jacket sliding sheepishly down the windshield of a pizza van at a red light, waving one huge paw at a startled driver, a teenager grinning from the passenger window

failure.text: The wind steals every word. All the Beast hears is the muscle car full of chanting linebackers, so it gives them a show: it rips the fiberglass pizza clean off the roof and hurls it like a discus into a cow pasture. The linebackers go wild. Lyle weeps a little.
failure.art: A huge wolf in a letterman jacket hurling a giant fiberglass pizza like a discus off a speeding van into a moonlit cow pasture, football players whooping from a muscle car, startled cows

signature.title: The Howling Deal of the Year
signature.place: Delaney Motors on Route 49, a midnight commercial shoot
signature.text: Duke Delaney is filming a TV spot at midnight on his car lot, under strings of pennant flags, beside a waving inflatable tube man and a giant cardboard cutout of himself giving a thumbs-up. "Delaney men never back down!" he bellows at the camera, take after take. His son is supposed to be in the next shot. Instead you find Brick locked in the showroom restroom, shaving his forearms with his father's electric razor while the fur grows back faster than he can cut it. "I can't go out there," he whispers through the door. "Not like this."
signature.art: A used car lot at midnight under floodlights and strings of colored pennant flags, a waving inflatable tube man, a giant cardboard cutout of a grinning salesman giving a thumbs-up, a broad man with a crew cut in a sport coat shouting at a film camera on a tripod, and at the back of the glass showroom a teenager kneeling at a restroom door with a light under it, hard white floodlight, wide shot

choices.label: Sit down outside the door and tell him he's allowed to skip it

success.text: You sit on the cold showroom tile with your back against the door and tell him the truth: the commercial doesn't need him, and a guy can say no to his dad. The razor stops buzzing. After a long while, Brick laughs, wet and shaky. "He's gonna be so mad." "Probably," you say. Through the crack under the door, you watch the fur on his knuckles settle back into skin.
success.art: A teenager sitting on showroom floor tiles with their back against a restroom door, a sliver of light under the door showing a big hand with fur fading back to skin, shiny new cars gleaming in the dark showroom

failure.text: "You don't get it," Brick growls, and the growl isn't his. The razor clatters into the sink. The restroom door bulges on its hinges, and out on the lot Duke yells, "Brick! You're up, son!" The howl that answers him shakes every pennant flag on Route 49.
failure.art: A restroom door bulging on its hinges in a dark car showroom, claw tips curling around its edge, a dropped electric razor on the tiles, pennant flags whipping on the floodlit lot outside

choices.label: Put on the lot's old wolf-mascot suit and do the commercial yourself

success.text: Delaney Motors happens to own a moth-eaten wolf suit from a 1979 promotion, and you happen to have zero shame. You burst onto the lot howling, slide across the hood of a station wagon and bellow, "Deals so good they're HOWLING!" The camera crew loses it. Duke, baffled, keeps the take. In the restroom, Brick laughs so hard he forgets to turn into anything.
success.art: A teenager in a moth-eaten wolf mascot costume sliding across the hood of a station wagon on a floodlit car lot, a camera crew doubled over laughing, a baffled broad salesman in a blazer

failure.text: Halfway through your hood slide, the wolf head pops off and rolls across the lot, and Duke stops the shoot to scream at everyone about professionalism. The louder he gets, the louder the restroom door rattles, until it gives and something huge crashes out through the showroom's back door.
failure.art: A mascot wolf head rolling across a floodlit car lot, a red-faced salesman yelling at a film crew, a huge shadowy wolf crashing out the back door of a car showroom

choices.label: Sneak behind the camera van and kill the floodlights

success.text: You find the generator behind the camera van and flip it off. The lot drops into darkness, the tube man sags over like it fainted, and Duke spends twenty minutes yelling at a generator. That's all Brick needs. He slips out the restroom window and away down the drainage ditch, and he looks back at you once, in the dark, still mostly a boy.
success.art: A dark car lot with a sagging inflatable tube man slumped over, a salesman yelling at a silent generator, a tall teenage boy with furry forearms slipping out a small restroom window into a ditch

failure.text: You trip over the cables and yank the cardboard Duke face down onto the camera. The real Duke turns, sees you sprawled on the asphalt, and the floodlights swing your way. The whole crew chases you off the lot, and behind you something in the showroom starts howling along with the car alarms.
failure.art: A teenager sprawled on asphalt tangled in camera cables beside a toppled cardboard salesman cutout, floodlights swinging toward them, a film crew charging, car alarms flashing across the lot

signature.title: Torches and Pitchforks
signature.place: The edge of Crystal Woods, behind the quarry, after dark
signature.text: The Glimmer Falls Booster Club has decided to handle the wolf problem themselves before it ruins the Monster Bowl. Forty grown men in maroon windbreakers are marching into Crystal Woods with flashlights, rakes, a borrowed hunting dog and, for some reason, the silver-plated trophy bat from the 1966 state title. Booster president Ron Stavros is out front, shouting about real men protecting their town. You know who they are hunting. So does the shaking, furry shape curled up in the drainage culvert at your feet.
signature.art: A line of grown men in maroon windbreakers marching into dark oak woods with flashlights, rakes and a silver-plated baseball bat, a hound straining on a leash, and in the foreground a teenager crouched beside a concrete drainage culvert where a huge gray furry shape in a torn letterman jacket trembles in the dark pipe, flashlight beams cutting through the trees, wide shot

choices.label: Record a howl and lead the mob the wrong way

success.text: You record your best howl, crank the volume all the way and leave the recorder playing in a hollow log a quarter mile north. The Booster Club charges after it in a stampede of windbreakers, shouting directions at each other. In the culvert, the Beast lets out a long breath that sounds exactly like a kid exhaling after a test.
success.art: A tape recorder glowing inside a hollow log in dark woods, a stampede of men in maroon windbreakers with flashlights charging toward it, a teenager and a huge wolf peeking out of a culvert far behind

failure.text: Your howl comes out like a sick goose. The hunting dog knows the difference instantly and drags Ron Stavros straight toward the culvert, so you grab the Beast's huge paw and run, crashing through the brush with forty flashlights bobbing behind you.
failure.art: A teenager holding a huge wolf's paw sprinting through dark brush, forty flashlight beams bobbing behind them, a hound dragging a red-faced man in a maroon windbreaker

choices.label: Stand in front of the culvert and tell the Booster Club to go home

success.text: You step into the flashlight beams. Then Moose steps up beside you, all six-foot-five of him, knitting bag on one shoulder, and says, "That's my quarterback. You want him, you go through the line." The Booster Club shuffles. Ron Stavros sputters. One by one, forty grown men remember they have work in the morning. Behind you, a soft, gruff voice says, "Nobody ever blocked for me before."
success.alone: You step into the flashlight beams alone, plant your feet and say it loud: "That's our quarterback. You want him, you go through me." The Booster Club shuffles. Ron Stavros sputters. One by one, forty grown men remember they have work in the morning. Behind you, a soft, gruff voice says, "Nobody ever blocked for me before."
success.art: A teenager and a towering gentle lineman with a knitting bag standing shoulder to shoulder in flashlight beams before a drainage culvert, a crowd of men in maroon windbreakers lowering their rakes

failure.text: The Booster Club laughs at you, which is worse than yelling. Ron Stavros pats you on the head and tells you to run along home. Behind you the culvert erupts, and the Beast tears off into the woods with forty flashlights and a trophy bat crashing after it.
failure.art: A smirking man in a maroon windbreaker patting a teenager on the head in flashlight glare, a huge wolf bursting out of a culvert behind them and bounding into the dark woods

choices.label: Crawl into the culvert beside him and keep him calm until they pass

success.text: You crawl into the cold pipe beside a seven-foot wolf and put your hand on its shaking shoulder. You breathe slowly and loudly, and after a while it breathes with you. Flashlight beams sweep across the culvert mouth and move on. By the time the woods are quiet, the shoulder under your hand is wearing a letterman jacket and belongs to a very tired seventeen-year-old.
success.art: Inside a cold concrete drainage pipe, a teenager resting a hand on the shoulder of a tired quarterback in a letterman jacket, faint flashlight beams sweeping past the round opening

failure.text: The Beast panics at the first flashlight and bolts out the far end of the culvert, and you get wedged in the pipe at the shoulders. The Booster Club finds you instead, and you spend the rest of the night explaining to forty disappointed men why you were in a drainpipe.
failure.art: A teenager wedged at the shoulders in a concrete drainage pipe, a ring of men in maroon windbreakers shining flashlights at them with disappointed faces, a hound sniffing their sneakers

signature.title: Lock the Door
signature.place: The varsity locker room, the night before the Monster Bowl
signature.text: Brick calls you from the pay phone outside the locker room at eleven. "Please come," he says. "I can feel it coming, and I don't want to hurt anybody." You find him tied to a bench with jump ropes, half wolf and shaking. Then headlights sweep across the frosted windows. Duke Delaney's truck. Brick's eyes flare stadium white. "He can't see me like this."
signature.art: A dim high school locker room at eleven at night, a tall teenage quarterback half turned into a wolf, gray fur along his arms and jaw, tied to a wooden bench with jump ropes and shaking, a teenager standing in front of the door, truck headlights sweeping across the frosted windows from outside, single caged bulb, medium shot

choices.label: Stand in the doorway and tell Duke he has to wait

success.text: Duke is a big man used to doors opening for him. This one doesn't. "Your son asked for space," you say, voice wobbling and holding. Duke looks past you at the shaking, furred shape on the bench, and something in his face cracks like a frozen pond. He goes back to his truck and sits there, and doesn't drive away.
success.art: A teenager blocking a locker room doorway with arms spread before a broad middle-aged man in a car-dealer blazer, his stern face beginning to crumple

failure.text: Duke moves you aside like a traffic cone. He sees his son, and before he can say a word, Brick snaps the jump ropes, crashes through the back door and is gone into the night, howling. Duke stands in the empty locker room holding a frayed rope and says nothing at all.
failure.art: A broad man standing alone in a locker room holding a snapped jump rope, a burst-open back door showing a dark field and a fleeing wolf shape

choices.label: Hide Brick in the equipment cage and bluff

success.text: You stack tackling dummies in front of the cage, kill the lights and tell Duke the janitor already locked up. He grumbles off. Inside the cage, Brick laughs, a real, wet, startled laugh, the first you've heard from him all week. Laughing, he looks a lot less like a wolf.
success.art: A chain-link equipment cage stacked with tackling dummies in a dark locker room, a half-wolf quarterback inside laughing with a hand over his mouth

failure.text: A tackling dummy topples. Duke hits the lights and sees fur through the chain-link. "Son?" Brick hears the disappointment before Duke even finishes the word, and the change slams through him. The cage door bends like a paper clip, and you chase a howl across the parking lot.
failure.art: A chain-link cage door bent outward in a brightly lit locker room, a toppled tackling dummy, a stunned father in the doorway

signature.title: Playing Hurt
signature.place: The trainer's room in the Glimmer Falls High field house, 1 a.m.
signature.text: A light is on in the field house trainer's room at one in the morning, and through the wired glass you can see something huge sitting on the taping table. It is the Beast, letterman jacket in ribbons, trying to tape its own swollen paw with a roll of athletic tape and its teeth. It keeps missing. A cassette recorder on the counter plays a man's voice on a loop: "Delaneys play hurt. Delaneys play hurt." The ice bath in the corner has frozen solid. The Beast hears you at the door, and its ears go flat.
signature.art: A high school athletic trainer's room at one in the morning under a single hanging lamp, a hulking gray wolf in a shredded maroon letterman jacket sitting on a padded taping table trying to wrap a swollen paw with a roll of white athletic tape held in its teeth, a cassette recorder on the counter, a steel ice bath frozen solid in the corner, a teenager peeking through the wired glass of the door, the wolf's ears flat against its head, warm lamp light, medium shot

choices.label: Hold out your hand for the tape and wrap the paw properly

success.text: After a long, rumbling minute, the Beast hands you the tape. You wrap the swollen paw the way the school nurse wraps a sprained wrist, snug and careful, and tell it, "You should sit out a game. That's allowed." The Beast looks down at the neat white wrap. Then, very softly, it whines, the sound a kid makes when a grown-up finally says the thing they needed to hear.
success.art: A teenager carefully wrapping white athletic tape around a huge furry wolf paw on a taping table at night, the wolf in a torn letterman jacket watching with soft drooping ears

failure.text: You reach for the tape and the Beast snatches its paw back with a snarl. "WALK IT OFF," roars the recorder, or the Beast, or both. It shoulders past you and limps off across the dark practice field, favoring the paw, and you are left holding a roll of tape and shaking.
failure.art: A huge limping wolf in a shredded letterman jacket crossing a dark practice field at night, a shaken teenager in a lit field house entrance holding a roll of athletic tape

choices.label: Hit STOP on the recorder and put on something else

success.text: You hit STOP. The voice cuts off mid-word. In the drawer under the counter you find the trainer's relaxation cassette, Sounds of the Pacific Shore, and pop it in. Waves wash through the room. The Beast's shoulders drop an inch, then two. By the time the tide comes in on side A, it has curled up on the taping table with its sore paw on an ice pack, snoring like a sleepy linebacker.
success.art: A huge wolf in a torn letterman jacket curled up asleep on a taping table, its paw resting on an ice pack, a cassette recorder playing on the counter, a teenager tiptoeing away

failure.text: You hit STOP and the recorder keeps playing anyway, louder: "Delaneys play hurt! Delaneys play hurt!" The Beast surges up off the table, the frozen ice bath cracks like a dropped tray, and you dive behind a stack of tackling dummies while it tears out the back door into the night.
failure.art: A teenager diving behind tackling dummies as a huge wolf in a letterman jacket bursts out the back of a trainer's room at night, shards of a cracked ice bath scattering across the tile

choices.label: Back out slowly and wedge the door shut with a bench

success.text: You back out one step at a time, without blinking, ease the door shut and wedge a bench under the handle. Inside, the snarling stops, and the Beast goes back to fumbling with the tape. When the janitor unlocks the room at dawn, he finds only a seventeen-year-old asleep on the taping table, his hand wrapped in a huge lopsided ball of tape.
success.art: A janitor at dawn finding a sleeping teenage quarterback on a taping table in a trainer's room, his hand wrapped in a huge lopsided ball of athletic tape, a wooden bench wedged against the entrance

failure.text: The bench screeches on the tile. The door bursts open, the Beast barrels past, and you go spinning into a laundry cart full of sweaty towels. You ride the cart across the field house floor straight into the trophy case, which chimes like a xylophone as every trophy wobbles.
failure.art: A teenager careening in a laundry cart full of towels across a field house floor toward a glass trophy case at night, a huge wolf in a letterman jacket bounding past

signature.title: Wolfmania
signature.place: Sports Hut at Starlight Mall, the late-night autograph table
signature.text: Word about the wolf has gotten around, and the town loves it. Sports Hut at Starlight Mall is selling WOLF PACK T-shirts as fast as it can print them, the line for Brick Delaney's autograph table snakes past the fountain, and Duke Delaney is out front shaking hands like he's running for mayor. Brick sits behind a stack of glossy photos, sweating through his letterman jacket, signing the same name over and over while the line chants, "Do the howl! Do the howl!" Every time they chant, the hand holding his pen sprouts a little more fur. He finds your face in the line, and his eyes say help.
signature.art: A crowded 1980s mall sporting goods store at night, a long line of fans in gray wolf T-shirts snaking out past a fountain, a sweating tall teenage quarterback in a maroon letterman jacket at a folding autograph table with a stack of glossy photos, gray fur sprouting on the hand holding his pen, his broad crew-cut father shaking hands nearby, a teenager in the line, bright store light, wide shot

choices.label: Get to the front of the line and ask him something nobody else is asking

success.text: When it's your turn you slide your T-shirt across the table and ask, "What do you actually like? Not football. Anything." Brick stares at you. The chant fades in his ears. "Old movies," he says finally, very quietly. "The ones where people just dance down the street for no reason." The fur on his hand settles back into skin. On your shirt he signs, small and careful: Brick. Just Brick.
success.art: A teenage quarterback at a mall autograph table talking quietly with a teenager across the table, his hand ordinary again, a long line of fans blurring behind them

failure.text: You ask what he likes, but Duke leans in over his shoulder before Brick can answer. "Winning!" Duke booms. "Right, son?" Brick's pen snaps in his fist. He signs your shirt in four claw marks that go clean through the fabric, and the line cheers like it's the best thing they've ever seen.
failure.art: A teenage quarterback at a mall autograph table gripping a snapped pen with clawed fingers, his booming father leaning over his shoulder, a crowd of fans cheering

choices.label: Work the line from the back with a rumor that he's moved to the food court

success.text: You and Lou work the line from the back: "He moved! Food court! Free photos!" The rumor runs up the line like a lit fuse, and in a minute the whole crowd stampedes toward the pretzel stand. Brick blinks at the sudden open space in front of his table, grabs his jacket and slips out the service hallway. On his way past, he squeezes your shoulder with a hand that is completely human.
success.art: A crowd stampeding toward a mall food court pretzel stand, a teenage quarterback in a letterman jacket slipping into a service hallway behind an abandoned autograph table, two teenagers grinning

failure.text: The rumor gets twisted on its way up the line, and by the time it reaches the front, everyone thinks the wolf is about to appear. The crowd surges forward chanting, the table tips, and Brick bolts into the stockroom. From behind the curtain comes a howl that rattles every rack of WOLF PACK T-shirts in the store.
failure.art: A toppled autograph table in a crowded mall sporting goods store, glossy photos scattered, racks of wolf T-shirts rattling as a huge furry shadow looms behind a stockroom curtain

choices.label: Jump up on the table and turn the chant into a conga line

success.text: You hop up on the autograph table and start a conga. "One, two, three, KICK!" The line, which will chant anything, happily follows you in a loop around the fountain, kicking. Brick watches from behind his stack of photos and laughs so hard his eyes water, and when the conga comes back around he gets up and joins the end of it, kicking higher than anybody.
success.art: A teenager leading a kicking conga line of fans in wolf T-shirts around a mall fountain, a laughing teenage quarterback in a letterman jacket joining the end of the line

failure.text: You climb onto the table and slip on a stack of glossy photos. You go down in a shower of Brick's smiling face, the line howls with laughter, and the laughter turns back into the chant, louder. Mall security walks you out past Duke, who gives you the look he saves for a fumble.
failure.art: A teenager slipping off an autograph table in a shower of glossy photos in a crowded mall store, mall security guards approaching, a big man in a sport coat glaring

signature.title: The Tower Climb
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls water tower beside the KGLM booth, the night before the Monster Bowl
signature.text: Every year on the night before the big game, the varsity seniors make the freshmen climb the water tower beside the KGLM booth and paint their jersey numbers on the tank to prove they're men. Tonight a dozen freshmen are strung along the ladder in the wind, frozen, while the seniors at the bottom chant "CLIMB! CLIMB! CLIMB!" Brick Delaney, team captain, is supposed to be waiting on the catwalk with the paint. Instead a seven-foot wolf in a cracked helmet crouches against the full moon, howling, and the freshman on the top rung can't go up or down.
signature.art: A tall water tower beside a small radio station at night under a huge full moon, a dozen terrified freshman boys clinging to the tower ladder in the wind, varsity seniors in maroon letterman jackets chanting at the base, and on the catwalk a seven-foot gray wolf in a cracked maroon football helmet crouched against the moon howling, a teenager climbing the ladder past the freshmen, silver moonlight, low wide shot

choices.label: Climb past the freshmen to the catwalk and talk to the Beast face to face

success.text: You climb past twelve shaking freshmen, telling each one, "You're fine, hold on," and pull yourself onto the catwalk beside a seven-foot wolf. It turns its huge head toward you. "You don't have to be up here either," you say. The Beast sits down heavily, legs dangling over the town, and lets the kid on the top rung climb down past it. By the time the last freshman reaches the ground, its paws are hands again, holding a paint can he never opened.
success.art: A teenager sitting beside a seven-foot wolf in a cracked football helmet on a water tower catwalk under a full moon, freshmen climbing safely down the ladder below, town lights spread out beneath

failure.text: Halfway up, the wind gusts and the whole ladder hums. You freeze between two freshmen, all three of you hugging the same rung while the Beast howls overhead and the seniors chant louder. The fire department gets everyone down at two a.m., and the Gazette runs a photo of you being carried down a ladder.
failure.art: A fire truck ladder reaching up a water tower at night, firefighters helping a teenager and two clinging freshmen down, a wolf howling at the full moon from the catwalk above

choices.label: Call off the climb and tell the seniors there's a new tradition

success.text: You step into the middle of the chanting seniors and yell up the ladder, "Everybody come down! New tradition: you don't have to prove anything to play!" Moose plants himself beside you, arms folded, and says, "Seconded." The chant falters. One senior, then three, go to the ladder and start helping freshmen down rung by rung. Up on the catwalk the howling stops, and the wolf watches, ears forward, as the team carries its youngest players down instead of daring them up.
success.alone: You step into the middle of the chanting seniors and yell up the ladder, "Everybody come down! New tradition: you don't have to prove anything to play!" A freshman clinging to the third rung yells, "Seconded!" The chant falters. One senior, then three, go to the ladder and start helping freshmen down rung by rung. Up on the catwalk the howling stops, and the wolf watches, ears forward, as the team carries its youngest players down instead of daring them up.
success.art: Varsity seniors in letterman jackets helping freshmen down a water tower ladder at night, a teenager and a big gentle lineman with folded arms at the base, a wolf on the catwalk listening with ears forward

failure.text: The seniors laugh you off. "Says who?" The chant starts again, louder, and on the catwalk the Beast throws back its head and howls along until the tank rings like a bell. A freshman starts crying on the ladder, and you have to climb up after him yourself, slow and shaking.
failure.art: A teenager climbing a water tower ladder after a crying freshman at night, laughing seniors at the base, a wolf in a cracked helmet howling at the full moon from the catwalk

choices.label: Pound on the KGLM booth and get Mix to put it on the air

success.text: Mix takes one look and keys the microphone. "Attention, parents of the Glimmer Falls Prospectors varsity squad: your sons are currently on the water tower. Repeat, the water tower." Within ten minutes a parade of station wagons roars up the access road, headlights blazing, moms in curlers leaning out the windows. The seniors scatter like pigeons. In the confusion the Beast slides down the far side of the tank and away into the dark, still mostly a boy.
success.alone: The night jock takes one look and keys the microphone. "Attention, parents of the Glimmer Falls Prospectors varsity squad: your sons are currently on the water tower. Repeat, the water tower." Within ten minutes a parade of station wagons roars up the access road, headlights blazing, moms in curlers leaning out the windows. The seniors scatter like pigeons. In the confusion the Beast slides down the far side of the tank and away into the dark, still mostly a boy.
success.art: A line of station wagons with blazing headlights roaring up an access road to a water tower at night, mothers in curlers leaning out, seniors scattering, a grinning radio host in a lit booth

failure.text: Mix puts it on the air, but the first truck up the access road is Duke Delaney's. He gets out, looks up, sees what is crouched on the catwalk and shouts, "Son, get down here and act like a man!" The howl that answers him rattles the whole tower and every station wagon behind him.
failure.alone: The night jock puts it on the air, but the first truck up the access road is Duke Delaney's. He gets out, looks up, sees what is crouched on the catwalk and shouts, "Son, get down here and act like a man!" The howl that answers him rattles the whole tower and every station wagon behind him.
failure.art: A big man in a sport coat shouting up at a water tower from beside his pickup truck at night, a wolf on the catwalk howling back at the moon, a teenager by the radio booth wincing

finale.title: The Monster Bowl
finale.text: Fourth quarter, Halloween night, and the full moon has come up over the scoreboard like a spotlight. The Prospectors are down by six. Coach Hollings is screaming, the stands are chanting BE A MAN, and on the fifty-yard line Brick Delaney comes apart in front of three thousand people: shoulder pads splitting, jersey 33 shredding, a seven-foot wolf in a cracked maroon helmet howling at the moon. The crowd thinks it's part of the show. Then it charges the stands where Duke is sitting.
finale.art: A small-town football stadium on Halloween night under a huge full moon rising over the scoreboard, a seven-foot gray wolf in shredded shoulder pads, a torn maroon jersey and a cracked maroon football helmet charging toward packed bleachers, a marching band scattering, four teenagers in homemade Halloween costumes racing onto the field toward it, one holding a pair of old tap shoes, white floodlight, wide shot

choices.label: Tackle the Beast at the twenty before it reaches the stands

success.text: You hit it low, the way Moose taught you, and Moose hits it high, and the Beast goes down in a spray of turf. Under the pile it shrinks and shrinks until it's just Brick, out cold in shredded pads. The crowd goes wild. It goes down as the greatest tackle in Glimmer Falls history, and nobody asks why he was a wolf.
success.alone: You hit it low and hard, all your weight behind your shoulder, and the Beast goes down in a spray of turf. Under you it shrinks and shrinks until it's just Brick, out cold in shredded pads. The crowd goes wild. It goes down as the greatest tackle in Glimmer Falls history, and nobody asks why he was a wolf.
success.art: A teenager and a huge lineman tackling a giant wolf on a moonlit football field in a spray of turf, the wolf shrinking back into a boy in torn shoulder pads

failure.text: It's like tackling a pickup truck. The Beast flicks you away, and you sail into the marching band's tuba section. When you sit up, dizzy, it has reached the stands, the chant is louder than ever, and the Beast is still growing.
failure.art: A teenager tumbling into a marching band's tuba section on a football sideline, a giant wolf climbing the stadium railing toward the crowd

choices.label: Kill the stadium lights and play something soft over the PA

success.text: You throw the breaker. The lights die, the chant falters, and in the dark the PA crackles into a scratchy old record: a tap number from 1946, all brushes and clarinet. The Beast stops at the railing, swaying, and slumps down on the track to listen. When the lights come back, he's Brick, curled up asleep, and the town is too spooked to finish the game.
success.art: A darkened stadium lit only by the moon, a giant wolf slumped peacefully on the running track beside the railing, an old record player glowing in the press box

failure.text: The breaker sparks and the lights stay on. The PA blares the fight song instead, the crowd roars along, and the Beast roars louder. Its claws hit the railing three feet from Duke, who doesn't run. He just stares, as every flashbulb in the stands goes off at once.
failure.art: A giant wolf with its claws on a stadium railing inches from a frozen middle-aged man, a hundred flashbulbs firing in the bleachers, sparks from a press box breaker

choices.label: Walk onto the field with the tap shoes, the notebook and the yearbook

success.text: You walk out to the fifty with Featherfoot's tap shoes, Brick's notebook and Duke's yearbook, and you hold up the shoes. The Beast stops. Then Duke climbs over the railing and walks onto the field in front of the whole town. He takes the yearbook and tears out his own page. "I was wrong," he says. "You don't have to be anything. You're my kid." The Beast sits down on the turf and cries, and as it cries it gets smaller, until a boy in torn pads is sobbing into his father's jacket.
success.art: A moonlit football field, a teenager holding up old tap shoes, a broad father kneeling to hug a sobbing quarterback in torn pads, the last wisps of wolf fur drifting away, a hushed crowd in the stands

failure.text: The Beast swats the notebook out of your hands, and its pages scatter across the field like confetti. Everything you brought is true, but Brick can't hear it over three thousand people chanting for him to be something else. You need the crowd to go quiet first.
failure.art: Notebook pages of dance diagrams scattering across a floodlit football field, a teenager reaching after them while a towering wolf roars at a chanting crowd

choices.label: Call a time-out, like the first nights, and tell the Beast it can sit this one out

success.text: The first nights of the week taught you that under all that fur the Beast is still a kid who has never once been allowed a break. So you give it one. You grab the referee's whistle, blow it as hard as you can and make a T with your hands at midfield. "TIME-OUT! Water break!" Three thousand people go quiet in confusion. The Beast skids to a stop on the twenty, chest heaving, trained to the bone. Then it sits down on the Prospectors' bench and stays there, shrinking, while the officials argue and the clock stops for good.
success.art: A teenager at midfield of a night football stadium making a time-out T with their hands, a whistle in their mouth, a huge wolf in torn shoulder pads sitting on the team bench, a hushed crowd under a full moon

failure.text: The whistle shrieks, but the chant is louder, and the Beast barrels past the bench without a glance. You get a yellow flag thrown at your feet and a long, scolding look from the head referee, but the game is not over, and neither are you.
failure.art: A huge wolf in a cracked maroon helmet charging past a team bench toward packed stadium bleachers at night, a teenager with a whistle beside a yellow penalty flag on the turf

choices.label: Stand up to the chant the way you did all week, and turn the stands around

success.text: All week the town chanted at Brick, and all week you answered back. You climb onto the rail in front of the stands, right in the Beast's path, and shout it the way you have before: "BE YOURSELF!" The Beast pulls up short three feet away. Behind you your crew takes it up, then the cheer squad, then whole sections of the bleachers, until three thousand people are shouting the new words instead of the old ones. The Beast drops to all fours, then to its knees, and the fur pours off it like rain until Brick is kneeling on the track, breathing.
success.art: A teenager standing on a stadium railing shouting with raised fists, a huge wolf in torn shoulder pads stopped short on the track, rows of fans in the bleachers on their feet shouting along under floodlights

failure.text: You climb onto the rail and shout, but the chant swallows you whole, and the Beast vaults the rail beside you without slowing. You topple backward into the front row's popcorn. Not your finest play, but you are on your feet in a heartbeat, and the game is still on.
failure.art: A teenager toppling backward off a stadium railing into a shower of popcorn in the front row, a huge wolf in a cracked helmet vaulting the rail beside them, floodlights blazing

choices.label: Block for him like the night before the game, and give his father room to walk out

success.text: The night before the Monster Bowl, somebody finally stood between Brick and everyone who wanted the wolf. You do it again. You walk out to the fifty with Featherfoot's tap shoes, the notebook and Duke's yearbook and stand between the Beast and three thousand people. "He's done for tonight," you say. The Beast stops. Up in the stands, Duke Delaney sees someone else's kid protecting his son, and it breaks something open. He climbs over the railing, walks onto the field and tears his own page out of the yearbook. "I was wrong. You're my kid. That's all you ever had to be." The Beast sits down on the turf and cries, and with every sob it gets smaller, until a boy in torn pads is crying into his father's jacket.
success.art: A big middle-aged man in a sport coat hugging a crying teenage quarterback in torn shoulder pads at the fifty-yard line under a full moon, a teenager holding old tap shoes beside them, a hushed stadium crowd

failure.text: You walk out to midfield with everything you found, but the stands are roaring, Duke is frozen in his seat, and the Beast cannot see past the floodlights to the boy you are trying to reach. It circles you, ears back, waiting for someone else to step out too.
failure.art: A teenager standing at midfield holding tap shoes and an old yearbook under blazing floodlights, a huge wolf in a cracked helmet circling them, a big man frozen in the bleachers

best.title: Featherfoot Junior
best.text: On the first Saturday in November, the Glitter Box revue has a new act. Brick Delaney, in Featherfoot's tap shoes and a maroon sequined letterman jacket that Moose knitted the trim for, taps a routine he wrote in a notebook disguised as a playbook, and he is magnificent. Moose plays the snare. Glory cries through her lashes. Duke sits in the back row for the first number, then the third row, then the front, and by the finale he is on his feet. Brick still plays football. He also cries at movies now, out loud, and nobody on the team says a word except "same."
best.art: A tall teenage boy tap dancing joyfully on a glittery theater stage in a maroon sequined letterman jacket with knitted trim and big old black tap shoes, a huge lineman with a curly mullet playing a snare drum beside him, a drag queen in a magenta sequin gown crying happily and a broad crew-cut father standing and cheering in the front row, warm stage spotlight, wide shot

good.title: Final Score
good.text: The Beast never comes back, and Brick plays out the season like nothing happened, all clean spirals and polite interviews. The Prospectors win state. His father is very proud. Sometimes, walking past the Glitter Box at night, you see Brick standing across the street with his hands in his jacket pockets, looking at an old photo in the lobby, before he turns and walks home.
good.art: A tall teenage quarterback in a maroon letterman jacket standing alone on a dark sidewalk at night with his hands in his pockets, looking across the street at a lit theater lobby window where an old black-and-white photo of a leaping dancer hangs, a streetlight above him, medium wide shot

bittersweet.title: Howl at the Moon
bittersweet.text: Brick is human again by November, but he quits the team and moves to his aunt's in Fresno before Thanksgiving without saying goodbye to anyone. Duke puts the house up for sale. On full moons you hear a howl from the foothills, not angry anymore, only lonely. You leave your porch light on, in case he ever wants to come back and try being soft.
bittersweet.art: A full moon over dark foothills behind a quiet suburb, a lone wolf silhouette standing on a ridge, and below a split-level house with a realtor stake on the lawn and a single porch light glowing on the house next door, silver moonlight, wide shot

bad.title: Man of the House
bad.text: The Beast wins the Monster Bowl single-handed, and nobody ever sees Brick Delaney again, only the thing in jersey 33 that the town keeps cheering for. And you? You wake up on November first in a letterman jacket that won't come off. You do two hundred push-ups before breakfast. When your crew asks if you're okay, you say "walk it off," and you can't remember ever saying anything else.
bad.art: A teenager with a blank hard stare doing push-ups on a bedroom floor in a maroon letterman jacket, three worried friends crowded in the doorway, and through the window a distant stadium with a gray wolf shape howling on top of the scoreboard under the moon, flat lamp light, medium shot
